opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as two axes that alternate in driving progress, and the interesting moments come when one axis gets stuck and the other has to unlock it.

The first is the modality axis: what kind of data the model sees and produces. We started with pure text, moved to image understanding, then to image generation, and now to video, speech and interleaved multimodal input and output. The second is the training-method axis: how we extract intelligence from that data. First came large-scale pretraining with next-token prediction, then supervised fine-tuning and RLHF for alignment, and more recently reinforcement learning on reasoning, the o1-style long chain of thought.

Looking back, the pattern is roughly this. When a new training method appears, it usually shows up first in language, because language is the most compressed and most "intelligent" modality. Text is already a product of human thinking, so the signal-to-noise ratio for learning reasoning is very high. Next-token prediction on text gave us GPT-style generalization. RL on text gave us long-chain reasoning. In both cases text came first.

Vision and other modalities are different. Images and video carry enormous information, but most of it is perceptual rather than conceptual. For years in computer vision we hoped that scaling generative or contrastive pretraining on images would produce the same kind of emergent intelligence we saw in language. Honestly, it didn't really happen. You get better representations and better generation quality, but not the jump in reasoning. My interpretation is that the pixel distribution is not aligned with the abstractions we care about. Modeling pixels well does not force the model to understand.

So the frontier question becomes: can the training-method advances we made in language transfer to other modalities? Can multimodal models do real long-chain reasoning in visual space, rather than translating images into text and then reasoning in text? I think that is one of the most important open problems right now. We're seeing early signs: models that think while looking, that zoom in, crop, re-examine, almost like a human scanning a picture. That's a training-method idea, RL with chain of thought, applied to a modality that previously only had pretraining.

There is also a deeper unification question. Today understanding and generation are still somewhat separate in vision. In language they are the same thing: the model that predicts the next token also understands. In vision we haven't found that single objective yet. If we do, if generation and understanding truly merge in the visual domain, I think that will be the next big leap. It would let models build something like a world model, simulate and plan, instead of just describing.

So to summarize: modalities expand what the model can perceive and act on, while training methods determine how much intelligence it can extract. Historically language led on methods and other modalities followed. The next phase, I believe, will be when methods that work in language, especially reinforcement learning and long reasoning, become native to vision and the physical world. That's where I expect the most interesting breakthroughs.

r001.rationale: It describes modalities and training methods as two axes that alternate in driving progress, with one unlocking progress when the other gets stuck.

r002.rationale: It says image pretraining did not produce a comparable reasoning leap, but does not present this and language reasoning research as a shared conclusion that compression-based training is insufficient.

r003.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning for reasoning but does not distinguish it from compression-based training by saying RL directly optimizes objectives.

r004.rationale: It presents multimodal reasoning and unifying visual understanding with generation as open problems, but does not say reasoning models made integrating multimodal generation and understanding more tractable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to see it is that modality and training method have been taking turns driving the field, and they're actually coupled more tightly than people usually assume.

If you look back at the whole arc, language got there first, and it got there first for a reason that has nothing to do with language being special. Text was the modality where the data was already dense with "reasoning signal." Human beings had already compressed their thinking into tokens, and the internet handed us trillions of them. So next-token prediction, which is an almost embarrassingly simple training objective, turned out to be enough. The training method could be simple because the modality was doing a lot of the work.

Vision was the opposite situation. We had enormous amounts of visual data, but the data is low in information density per unit. A pixel doesn't carry a thought. So the community spent years trying to force the language recipe onto images, predicting pixels, predicting patches, and it never produced the same kind of emergent capability. In my view that's not a failure of scale, it's a mismatch. For vision, the modality is "cheap" and the training method has to be smart. You need the objective to extract structure that isn't explicitly written down, which is why things like contrastive learning, masked modeling, and later generative objectives mattered so much more in vision than in language.

So I'd put it this way: the harder the modality is to supervise naturally, the heavier the burden on the training method. And conversely, when a modality provides rich natural supervision, you can get away with very naive training and let compute carry you.

The really interesting phase is now, when the two start to feed back on each other. Once you have a strong language model, the training method for other modalities changes. You no longer need vision to learn semantics from scratch, you can align it to a space that already encodes concepts. That's why multimodal models arrived so quickly after language models matured. The advance in one modality effectively became a new training method for the others.

And I think the next step runs the other way. Language models are hitting a wall on data, and the obvious reserve of data is in the physical world, video, embodiment, interaction. But that data won't come with labels or with tidy next-token structure. So the pressure is going to shift back onto training methods, things like reinforcement learning, self-play, world models, learning from outcomes rather than from imitation. In that sense, I don't see modality and method as two separate tracks. Each time one of them saturates, it hands the problem to the other.

r001.rationale: The response says modality and training method are tightly coupled, take turns driving the field, and feed back on each other.

r002.rationale: It calls next-token prediction a mismatch for vision, but does not connect that conclusion to research on language reasoning or identify a shared conclusion about compression-based training.

r003.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning and learning from outcomes, but does not distinguish RL from compression-based training by direct optimization of objectives.

r004.rationale: It discusses multimodal models emerging after language models matured, but does not credit reasoning models with making multimodal generation and understanding more tractable.

astra-6.text:
I see them as two interacting dimensions. Modalities determine what a model can learn from and express—text, images, audio, video, and potentially actions. Training methods determine how effectively it can turn those signals into useful capabilities. So I wouldn’t describe the evolution of large models as simply adding more modalities, or simply finding better training algorithms. Each creates opportunities and demands for the other.

Take video. Adding video gives a model access to motion and changes over time, but access alone doesn’t guarantee that it learns causality or understands physical processes. That depends on the training objective, the data, and how we evaluate what it has learned. Likewise, an improvement in training can make information that was already present in the data much more usable.

There’s also an interesting tension: different modalities have different structures. Text is relatively discrete and already highly compressed by human language. Audio and video contain much more continuous information, including a lot that may be irrelevant to a particular task. We want training methods that can capture shared concepts across modalities without losing the details that make each modality useful.

So my view is that the strongest progress comes when the two develop together. A new modality expands the learning problem; a better training method makes that expansion productive. The meaningful question is whether their combination gives the model capabilities that generalize, rather than just another kind of input it can accept.

r001.rationale: The response says modalities create opportunities and demands for training methods, while better training makes expanded modalities productive, describing the two as developing together.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss compression-based training or identify a shared conclusion from research on next-token prediction across modalities and language reasoning.

r003.rationale: It does not mention reinforcement learning or distinguish it from compression-based training by direct objective optimization.

r004.rationale: It does not mention reasoning models or say they made multimodal generation and understanding problems more tractable.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as two forces that push each other forward. Adding a modality expands what a model can observe and learn from, while advances in training determine how effectively it can use that information.

Take video as an example. It gives a model access to motion, temporal relationships, and how events unfold. But simply feeding in more video doesn’t automatically produce a better understanding of the world. You need to decide how to represent it, what training objective to use, and how to connect it with language. Those are training questions prompted by a change in modality.

The relationship also works in the other direction. A more effective training method can make a modality useful at a scale or cost that wasn’t practical before. So I wouldn’t describe the evolution of large models as a sequence where modalities advance first and training methods follow. It’s a feedback loop.

The important distinction is between accepting more kinds of input and actually learning from their relationship. A model might process both images and text, but the deeper advance is when visual information improves its language understanding, and language helps it interpret what it sees. That’s where advances in modalities and training methods really come together.

r001.rationale: The response says modalities and training methods push each other forward and describes their relationship as a feedback loop.

r002.rationale: It does not mention compression-based training or the shared conclusion of research on next-token prediction and language reasoning.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss reinforcement learning or contrast its direct optimization of objectives with compression-based training.

r004.rationale: It does not credit reasoning models with making multimodal generation and understanding integration more tractable.
